chapter_theme: Kannaki pleads her husband's case before the Pandya: the queen's dream of the falling sceptre is told, Kannaki indicts the king as one who did not inquire and sets the Chola precedents of justice against him, the broken anklet proves her right, and the king, naming himself the thief, dies by his own sentence; three closing venbas restate the moral that dharma is death to the wrongdoer and credit the king's death to the sight and words of the wronged wife.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, who pleads his case before the Pandya
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as தென்னவன், செழியன், கொற்கை வேந்தன்)
the gatekeeper of the Pandya's palace
the queen's retinue of women and attendants

silappathikaram:20:1-7.reading: The Pandya queen tells a companion, line by line, the omens she saw in her sleep: the umbrella and sceptre falling, the gate bell trembling, the eight directions shaking, darkness swallowing the sun, a rainbow by night and stars dropping by day.
silappathikaram:20:1-7.nuance: Every omen is a disorder of the king's world or of the sky, and the first is the fall of the umbrella and sceptre, the signs of just rule; the refrain காண்பென்காண் எல்லா marks it as spoken to a companion. The lines stand in a block of their own, apart from the akaval that follows, and open with ஆங்குக், tying the scene to the moment Kannaki reaches the palace gate.
silappathikaram:20:1-7.event: The Pandya queen tells a companion her ill-omened dream of the king's umbrella and sceptre falling.

silappathikaram:20:8-33.reading: The queen, reading the dream as a coming harm to the king, goes to tell him, attended by women bearing mirror, jewels, cloth, colours, musk, garlands, fly-whisk and incense and by a crowd of hunchbacks and dwarfs, and tells her dream to the king seated on his lion throne.
silappathikaram:20:8-33.nuance: Lines 8 to 15 restate the omens in the queen's own words and end in her resolve (வருவதோர் துன்பமுண்டு, மன்னவற்கு யாம் உரைத்தும்), so the king is warned before the accuser arrives. The long list of what the attendants carry sets the full ceremony of the court against the lone woman with one anklet who comes next.
silappathikaram:20:8-33.event: The queen, with her retinue, goes to the king on his lion throne and tells him her evil dream.
silappathikaram:20:8-33.unit_note: End moved from line 28 to line 33: line 28 (ஈண்டுநீர் வையங்காக்கும்) runs on into line 29 (பாண்டியன்பெருந் தேவிவாழ்கென), and the queen's scene closes at line 33 with the king on his throne; இப்பால் there turns to Kannaki.

silappathikaram:20:34-54.reading: Kannaki bids the gatekeeper announce to the king who has strayed from right rule that a woman holding one anklet, who has lost her husband, is at the gate, and the gatekeeper, hailing the Pandya, tells him that a woman who is neither Kotravai nor Kali but seems as angry stands there.
silappathikaram:20:34-54.nuance: Kannaki's message already pronounces the verdict: the king is one whose mind has lost its wisdom and who has erred in the rule of kingship (இறைமுறை பிழைத்தோன்), which recalls the patikam's அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர். The gatekeeper denies she is the war goddess or Kali while piling up their images, preparing her later standing as a goddess, and hails the king as the Panchava who never walks with blame (பழியொடு படராப் பஞ்சவ) just before the blame falls.
silappathikaram:20:34-54.event: Kannaki asks the gatekeeper to announce her, and he tells the king that a widow holding one anklet, fierce as a goddess, waits at the gate.
silappathikaram:20:34-54.unit_note: Start moved from line 29 to 34 (the queen's scene closes at 33 with இப்பால்); end moved from line 53 to 54, since line 54 repeats the gatekeeper's refrain and closes his speech with என, while the core boundary fell between the refrain and its repetition.

silappathikaram:20:55-73.reading: Admitted at the king's word, Kannaki answers his question by calling him a king who did not inquire, recalls the Chola kings of her city who relieved a bird's distress and crushed their own son under the chariot wheel for a cow's grief, and names herself as the wife of Kovalan, who came to Madurai driven by former deeds and was killed at the king's order while selling her anklet.
silappathikaram:20:55-73.nuance: The plea gives two causes in one breath: she indicts the king as தேரா மன்னா, the one who failed to inquire, and yet says Kovalan entered Madurai because ஊழ்வினை drove him (line 69). The two Chola precedents (the kings are not named in the Tamil) set the standard of a justice that spares not even the king's own son, and they are her own city's kings, offered to a Pandya. The king's reply begins on the last line (பெண்ணணங்கே).
silappathikaram:20:55-73.event: Brought before the king, Kannaki names the Chola precedents of justice, her city, her husband's lineage and herself as the wife of the Kovalan he had killed.

claims.claim: a just king relieves the suffering even of a bird or a cow, though it cost his own son's life
a former deed drives a man to the place where it ripens
a king who punishes without inquiry fails in justice

silappathikaram:20:55-73.unit_note: Start moved from line 54 to 55: the gatekeeper's speech ends with என on line 54, and the king's summons (வருக மற்றவள்) begins the new scene.

silappathikaram:20:74-91.reading: The king answers that killing a thief is no cruel rule but royal justice; Kannaki says her anklet holds gems and the king that the queen's holds pearls; she breaks her anklet, a gem leaps to the king's mouth, and he, his umbrella lowered and sceptre slack, declares that he who heeded the goldsmith is no king but the thief, that the guarding of the southern land has failed first with him, prays his life to end and falls, while the queen, trembling, falls worshipping his feet.
silappathikaram:20:74-91.nuance: Where the patikam and the narrator of the killing scene give former deeds as the reason the king did not inquire, the king here names only his own fault, heeding the goldsmith's word (பொன்செய் கொல்லன் தன்சொற் கேட்ட), and sentences himself; karma and the king's fault both stand as causes in the story, and he takes the second. தாழ்ந்த குடையன் தளர்ந்தசெங் கோலன் fulfils the queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre. The queen's words before she falls (கணவனை இழந்தோர்க்குக் காட்டுவது இல்) can be read as 'there is nothing left to offer those who lose their husbands'; the line does not say outright that she dies.
silappathikaram:20:74-91.event: Kannaki breaks her anklet and a gem flies to the king's mouth; the king declares himself the thief, wishes his life ended and falls, and the queen falls at his feet.

claims.claim: to kill a thief is not cruel rule but the king's due justice
a king who punishes on a false word is himself the thief
a king whose guarding of the people has failed should not live

silappathikaram:20:92-95.reading: A closing venba says the saying of many assemblies, that dharma becomes death to those who do wrong, is not false, and bids the queen of the king who did the scarring wrong see what the speaker, a woman of harsh deeds, will do.
silappathikaram:20:92-95.nuance: வயவேந்தன் றேவி may be addressed (the queen is told to watch) or may be the subject (see what the queen does, and what I will do); the first-person கடுவினையேன் points to Kannaki, who opens the next kaathai calling the queen கோவேந்தன் தேவி and herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன், but the speaker is not named. The first line restates the patikam's first moral (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று) as a common saying now proved.

claims.claim: dharma itself becomes death to those who do wrong

silappathikaram:20:96-99.reading: A second venba says that seeing the tears from her blue-lily eyes, the lone anklet in her hand, her form like one whose life had left, and her dark hair spread like a forest, the lord of Koodal took fright and became a lifeless husk.
silappathikaram:20:96-99.nuance: The pun கூடலான் கூடு ஆயினான் (the lord of Koodal became a mere frame) makes the city's name the measure of the king's ruin. Here sight alone kills, not the king's own verdict of line 87. The first-person பாவியேன் is unexplained: it may be the poet's cry, or a speaker's who is not named.
silappathikaram:20:96-99.event: The Pandya, seeing Kannaki's tears, lone anklet and spread hair, dies of fear.

silappathikaram:20:100-103.reading: A third venba says that the lord of the Vaigai, at the sight of her dust-covered body, loosened hair, lone anklet and tears, lost, and when her words entered his ears, lost his life.
silappathikaram:20:100-103.nuance: தோற்றான் is said twice: he lost first as a party loses a case, at the sight of her (the kaathai is the telling of the case, வழக்குரை), and then lost his life at her words. The three venbas give three accounts of how the king died, by her power, against the akaval's self-sentence.
silappathikaram:20:100-103.event: The Pandya, beaten at the sight of Kannaki, dies on hearing her words.

links.note: The queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre is fulfilled in the king's lowered umbrella and slack sceptre at the verdict.
links.teaches: The omen comes first in the queen's private dream and is fulfilled the same hour in public, so the fall of justice is shown as already decided before Kannaki speaks.

links.note: Both use the falling star and the broken royal umbrella as signs of a king's death.
links.teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam stock of royal death-omens but moves them into a dream before the death, turning the elegist's after-the-fact proof of grief into a warning that comes too late to be heeded.

gains.a: its dream gains a traditional sense: these are the recognised signs that a king will die, not private fears
gains.b: the poem's omens gain a narrative use, where the same signs foretell a death caused by the king's own wrong

links.note: Kannaki vowed to see the cruel king and ask him the reason; here she stands at his gate and sends in her charge.
links.teaches: The vow made beside the body is kept as a legal summons through the gatekeeper, so her grief is shown taking the form of a formal case rather than a lament.

links.note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
links.teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

gains.a: Kannaki's precedent gains the weight of an established praise-formula of the Chola line
gains.b: the formula gains a use beyond flattery: it becomes the measure by which another king is judged

links.note: The narrator says the king did not inquire because it was the hour of karma's fruit (தேரான் ஆகி); Kannaki calls him the king who did not inquire (தேரா மன்னா).
links.teaches: The same failure to inquire is excused by karma in the narrator's voice and charged as guilt in Kannaki's, and she herself also names karma, so the epic holds both causes together rather than choosing one.

links.note: The couplet makes inquiry (தேர்ந்துசெய்) part of what justice is; Kannaki's first words to the king name him as the one who did not inquire.
links.teaches: The couplet treats inquiry as within the ruler's power, while the epic shows a ruler failing it in an hour the narrator calls karma's ripening, and still holds him answerable for it.

gains.a: Kannaki's charge gains a definition: what the king failed is the first step of justice itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: a king fails to inquire under the press of former deeds and is still judged by the couplet's standard

links.note: Kannaki dreamed that she spoke before the king and that harm came to the king and the city with him; here she speaks before the king and he falls.
links.teaches: Her dream foretold both the plea and the harm beyond the king, so the king's fall here is only the first part of what the dream foretold, with the city's burning still to come.

links.note: The narrator's venba says the never-bent sceptre bent as the fruit of former karma; the king says only that he heeded the goldsmith and is himself the thief.
links.teaches: The narrator assigns the bent sceptre to karma while the king, judging himself, assigns it wholly to his own act, so the epic lets the wrongdoer refuse the excuse its narrator offers.

links.note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
links.teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

gains.a: the king's self-sentence gains a rule behind it: ruin comes from within to the king who does not examine
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene that separates its two conditions, an accessible king who still fails to examine, and shows the ruin as self-inflicted in act as well as in result

links.note: The patikam's first moral, that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship, is restated here as a common saying proved true.
links.teaches: The moral announced at the outset as the poem's thesis is here called a saying of the assemblies now proved, so the book frames its plot as the demonstration of a received maxim.

links.note: The venba's 'queen of the king' and the speaker 'of harsh deeds' recur at the opening of the next kaathai, where Kannaki addresses the queen and calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன்.
links.teaches: The next kaathai's opening supports reading this venba as Kannaki's words to the queen, and shows the threat 'see what I will do' carried into the vow against the city.

links.note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the venba says dharma is death to the wrongdoer, but the speaker, who did no wrong, calls herself one of harsh deeds and the wrongdoer's queen suffers too.
links.teaches: The epic agrees that harm returns to the one who did it, but shows it spreading to the innocent queen and to the victim who names her own karma, so the couplet's neat return of pain to its doer becomes a wider ruin.

gains.a: the venba's maxim gains the couplet's general rule that harm returns to its doer
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where pain does reach the doer, yet also those around him, which its own wording does not consider

links.note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
links.teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

gains.a: the venba gains a moral law behind its marvel: tears of the wronged are a force against an unjust king
gains.b: the couplet gains an extreme case, where the weapon of tears acts at once and on the king's life, not slowly on his wealth

source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed line numbers run 14 behind from line 20 (printed 15) and end at 80 against 103 lines as shown.
Line 54 repeats line 53 (கணவனை இழந்தாள் கடையகத் தாளே): probably the gatekeeper's refrain, but possibly a doubled line.

Block labels: lines 1-7 carry no metre label ('-') and lines 8-91 are labelled கருப்பம், a label the other kaathais do not use; lines 1-7 are in a different refrain metre from the akaval of 32 onward, and lines 8-29 are in short lines, so the single கருப்பம் block spans more than one metre.
Line 73: Kannaki's speech ends and the king's reply (பெண்ணணங்கே) begins mid-line, so no unit boundary can fall on the speech change.
